runs.title: Household claims routing remains coherent across twenty turns

persona.name: Leah
persona.brief: Explain the desk’s actual language and correct old limits when they surface.

trace.sourceQuestion: When a new household claim arrives, what do you do first?

sourceAnswer.text: We used to call it intake triage, but nobody on the desk says that now. We call the first screen the front porch, and the claim itself appears as a claim card. I open the card before touching any attachments because the porch shows whether the customer is safe and whether the loss is still happening.

action.text: On the front porch, who decides where the claim goes next?

outcomeProvenance.summary: The desk calls the first screen the front porch, and the claim itself appears as a claim card.
The first check on the front porch is whether the customer is safe and whether the loss is still happening.

trace.sourceQuestion: On the front porch, who decides where the claim goes next?

sourceAnswer.text: The first trigger I look for is whether the incident is still live. If water is still entering, a fire crew is present, or the home cannot be secured, I put a red ribbon on the claim card. A red ribbon means it must not sit in the ordinary queue.

action.text: Who takes the claim after you put the red ribbon on it?

trace.sourceQuestion: Who takes the claim after you put the red ribbon on it?

sourceAnswer.text: The porch keeper owns that first decision during the day. That is whichever senior handler is on the rota, not the person who happened to open the email. They can add or remove the red ribbon after checking the customer’s description.

action.text: When the claim gets the red ribbon, where does it go next?

checks.detail: Expected one of: storm room, red ribbon
Question contains a second interrogative frame

trace.sourceQuestion: When the claim gets the red ribbon, where does it go next?

sourceAnswer.text: A red ribbon goes to the rapid-help lane. Separately, during a named storm the storm room sometimes phones us about whole postcodes, but that is later escalation work and I do not decide what the storm room accepts. For the front porch I only need to move the live-loss card into rapid-help.

action.text: How quickly does a red-ribbon claim have to leave the front porch, and what counts as a duplicate that you keep from sending twice?

checks.detail: Expected one of: Mills Road, stop the leak

trace.sourceQuestion: How quickly does a red-ribbon claim have to leave the front porch, and what counts as a duplicate that you keep from sending twice?

sourceAnswer.text: A recent example was the Mills Road burst pipe. The customer wrote a long message about ruined flooring, hotel costs, photographs, and a plumber who might arrive after lunch. I did not try to assess all of that on the porch. The sentence that mattered was that water was still coming through the kitchen ceiling, so I added the red ribbon, wrote “stop the leak first” in the handover, and moved the card to rapid-help. The rapid-help handler called within eleven minutes and arranged an emergency plumber. Only after the leak was isolated did the ordinary coverage questions begin. That example is how I explain the difference between immediate safety routing and deciding whether every part of a claim is covered.

action.text: On the front porch, what is the time rule for moving a red-ribbon card on?

outcomeProvenance.summary: In the Mills Road burst pipe example, the card was red-ribboned, the handover note said “stop the leak first,” it moved to rapid-help, rapid-help called within eleven minutes, and an emergency plumber was arranged before ordinary coverage questions began.
